title: Shrinking civic space and contested global rules are shifting the cost of dissent toward civil society while resistance adapts
source_unit: CIVICUS, 2026 State of Civil Society Report
geography: Global civil-society, civic-space, technology-governance, conflict, climate, migration, and gender-rights analysis

denominator.unit: global civil-society and civic-space assessment frame

restriction_pattern.value: civic space is described as increasingly restricted while activists, journalists, and ordinary people face rising costs of speaking out

funding_pressure.value: civil-society organizations face a funding crisis as state and philanthropic support collapses or becomes more conditional

trust_link.value: disconnection from communities can weaken support and make civic-space restrictions easier to impose

observations.method: CIVICUS global advocacy and civil-society synthesis drawing on country experiences, activist input, and thematic analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The report has an explicit civil-society advocacy standpoint and is not a probability sample or neutral causal index; country coverage, source selection, and normative framing shape comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Activists, journalists, human-rights defenders, community organizations, marginalized groups, funders, and people facing restrictions on association, expression, or assembly.
observations.counterinterpretation: Restrictions and funding pressure can coexist with legal wins, public mobilization, community support, and new forms of collective organization.

denominator.unit: global technology-governance assessment in the CIVICUS report

governance_gap.value: rapid generative-AI expansion has exposed a fragmented regulatory landscape

risk_set.value: AI and digital systems are linked to electoral disinformation, surveillance, military targeting, deepfake pornography, and hate-speech amplification

oversight_route.value: civil society is calling for human-rights-based global standards and a central role in oversight

observations.method: CIVICUS thematic analysis of technology, AI governance, civic rights, corporate accountability, and civil-society responses.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies risks and political claims rather than estimating the prevalence or causal effect of each technology application; examples are selected for advocacy relevance.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls targeted by digital abuse, journalists, activists, conflict-affected communities, technology workers, states, corporations, and regulators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital tools can support fact-checking, war-crime documentation, missing-person identification, and civic coordination when rights and accountability protections exist.

observations.period: 2026; global governance, international rules, and state power

rules_pressure.value: global governance rules and institutions are described as being tested by powerful states pursuing self-interest and disregarding international law

institutional_withdrawal.value: state withdrawals and reduced financial support are described as weakening multilateral and human-rights functions

civil_society_response.value: civil society calls for stronger accountability, broader representation, Security Council reform, and systematic participation in global processes

observations.method: CIVICUS analysis of global governance, conflict, international law, multilateral institutions, and civil-society advocacy.
observations.uncertainty: Claims about state motives, legal compliance, and institutional decline are interpretive and advocacy-oriented; the report does not provide a standardized causal measure of global-order effectiveness.
observations.subgroup: States with different power positions, international institutions, civil-society groups, human-rights defenders, conflict-affected populations, and communities dependent on multilateral protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: International institutions can adapt, states can cooperate selectively, and civil-society pressure can produce legal and policy gains even during geopolitical contestation.

observations.period: 2025-2026; resistance, youth mobilization, and external response

denominator.unit: global civil-society resistance and movement-response synthesis

movement_change.value: Gen Z movements are described as using collective leadership, decentralized decision-making, social media, and creative communications

response_tools.value: civil society uses fact-checking, litigation, early-warning systems, secure platforms, and community documentation to resist repression and misinformation

sustainability.value: sustaining resistance requires protecting people on the frontlines and avoiding movement exhaustion

observations.method: CIVICUS case synthesis of civic resistance, youth mobilization, technology use, litigation, and community-level responses.
observations.uncertainty: Examples of successful resistance do not establish generalizability, durability, or population-level political effects; movement visibility can be shaped by media and advocacy selection.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z activists, local organizers, journalists, human-rights defenders, communities targeted by disinformation, and civil-society networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Decentralization can improve resilience but may also create coordination, accountability, safety, and resource challenges.

related_sources.claim: CIVICUS launch summary emphasizes rising repression, shrinking civic space, and adaptive resistance.
CIVICUS Monitor provides complementary civic-space conditions and country-focused reporting.

boundary: This record adds an advocacy-informed geopolitical and state-consequences route linking civic space, technology governance, multilateral rules, repression, resistance, and external accountability. It is not a neutral country index, incident census, respondent political-attitudes dataset, or causal estimate of civic action or state behavior.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official CIVICUS 2026 report and launch materials were reviewed; civic-space, technology-governance, global-rules, resistance, and methodological-standpoint claims were cross-checked.
